content: Survival rates for childhood cancer have significantly improved due to advancements in treatment. However, these improved outcomes are accompanied by late-onset complications, including liver-related adverse effects. While liver complications are commonly observed during or shortly after treatment, the long-term risk of hepatic late adverse effects in childhood cancer survivors remains largely unknown. Understanding these risks and their associated factors is crucial for guiding future treatment decisions and follow-up care. This review aimed to assess the available evidence on the relationship between antineoplastic treatments—such as chemotherapy, radiotherapy involving the liver, liver surgery, and bone marrow transplantation (BMT)—and the development of hepatic late adverse effects in childhood cancer survivors. The search for relevant studies included databases like CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, as well as conference proceedings from SIOP and ASPHO. Studies were included if they examined hepatic late adverse effects occurring at least one year after the completion of treatment in patients diagnosed with cancer at 18 years of age or younger. Case reports, case series, and studies with fewer than 10 patients were excluded. The review included 33 cohort studies with a total of 7,876 participants. These studies investigated hepatic late adverse effects following antineoplastic treatment for various childhood cancers, including both hematological and solid malignancies. Methodological limitations were noted across all studies. The prevalence of hepatic late adverse effects, defined biochemically, varied widely from 0% to 84.2%. When focusing on studies that defined hepatic late adverse effects as alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels above the upper limit of normal (indicating cellular liver injury), the prevalence ranged from 5.8% to 52.8%. These studies had median follow-up durations ranging from 3 to 23 years after cancer diagnosis. A stricter definition of ALT levels exceeding twice the upper limit of normal yielded a prevalence range of 0.9% to 44.8% across five studies. One study examined biliary tract injury, defined by gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT) levels above the upper limit of normal and twice the upper limit of normal, reporting prevalences of 5.3% and 0.9%, respectively. Three studies assessed disturbances in biliary function, defined by elevated bilirubin levels, with prevalences ranging from 0% to 8.7%. Multivariable analyses from two studies indicated that radiotherapy involving the liver (particularly when a high percentage of the liver was irradiated), higher body mass index (BMI), longer follow-up duration, and older age at evaluation were associated with an increased risk of cellular liver injury. Additional factors that may elevate this risk include the use of busulfan, thioguanine, hepatic surgery, chronic hepatitis C infection, metabolic syndrome, statin use, non-Hispanic white ethnicity, and higher alcohol consumption (more than 14 units per week). Chronic hepatitis C was also identified as a risk factor in six univariable analyses. Furthermore, one study found that radiotherapy involving the liver, higher BMI, higher alcohol intake, longer follow-up duration, and older age at cancer diagnosis increased the risk of biliary tract injury. The prevalence of hepatic late adverse effects varied significantly among studies with adequate outcome definitions, ranging from 1% to 53%. Evidence suggests that radiotherapy involving the liver, higher BMI, chronic hepatitis C, and longer follow-up duration or older age at follow-up are significant risk factors for hepatic late adverse effects. Other potential risk factors include busulfan, thioguanine, hepatic surgery, higher alcohol intake, metabolic syndrome, statin use, non-Hispanic white ethnicity, and older age at cancer diagnosis. High-quality studies are needed to better understand the impact of treatment doses, time trends, and associated risk factors on the development of hepatic late adverse effects in childhood cancer survivors.
